claims.text: The nanoparticles are FeCuCrCoNi high-entropy alloy nanoparticles.
The FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles have a near-equiatomic composition.
Metadynamics or umbrella sampling can be used to compute nanoparticle free-energy landscapes across a range of sizes.
Molecular dynamics can investigate the thermal behavior of high-entropy alloy nanoparticles at the atomic scale.
Enhanced molecular dynamics can reveal size-dependent thermal stability in FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles.
Enhanced sampling can resolve subtle changes in transition barriers and thermal responses that conventional molecular dynamics may miss.
The nanoparticle free-energy landscape mediates thermal response through surface-energy contributions.
Multi-element interactions contribute to the thermal response of high-entropy alloy nanoparticles.
Enhanced molecular dynamics promotes sampling across thermal activation barriers.
Enhanced molecular dynamics enables sampling of rare events and free-energy minima.
Surface phenomena and atomic diffusion can produce temperature-dependent structural and chemical evolution in multicomponent alloy nanoparticles.
Smaller FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles will have free-energy profiles distinct from those of larger nanoparticles.
Smaller FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles will have lower thermal stability than larger nanoparticles.
The predicted lower thermal stability of smaller nanoparticles is caused by their higher surface-to-volume ratios.
Conventional molecular dynamics may provide an incomplete picture of size-dependent thermal stability because it may not resolve subtle free-energy differences.
Size-dependent thermal effects are most pronounced at nanoscale dimensions where surface effects dominate.
Size-dependent differences diminish as nanoparticles approach bulk dimensions.
Nanoparticle morphology and simulation parameters may affect calculated free-energy barriers and transition temperatures.
